name: Amazon
tagline: Global retail marketplace with same-week delivery on roughly everything.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely one-shot an Amazon-shaped website: product grid, search, cart, checkout, order history. None of that is the product. Amazon is hundreds of fulfillment centers, millions of third-party sellers, a payments and returns machine, and a delivery network that puts a spatula on your doorstep tomorrow. The software is the thin skin over the logistics. The closest honest personal build is a shopping list or price-watch tool that sits on top of Amazon rather than replacing it.
coreLoopDIY: A local price and wishlist tracker that watches product pages you paste in and tells you when something drops below your target.
requirements: Node runtime on a machine that stays on, or a cheap VPS
SQLite for stored items and price history
Product URLs you actually care about
Tolerance for scraping breakage and rate limits
whatYouLose: Actual inventory, warehouses and next-day delivery
Millions of third-party sellers and their long-tail catalog
Reviews, ratings and Q&A written by other buyers
Payments, fraud protection and no-argument returns
Anything resembling reliability, since page scraping breaks constantly
moatNotes: Two-sided liquidity plus physical logistics. Neither is a software problem you solve alone.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay Amazon because something arrives. The website is a catalog and a checkout button, both of which a coding agent can produce before lunch, but the value is the warehouse thirty miles away, the driver, the seller who stocked it, the refund that goes through without a phone call. No amount of clean code creates supply. The most a personal build can do is make you a smarter buyer inside the system: track prices, avoid fake discounts, keep a wishlist that is not designed to nudge you into buying now.
notes: The storefront is a one-sitting build; the parcel on your porch is not. The moat is physical logistics plus marketplace liquidity, neither of which ships in a git repo.
prompt:
Build a local price and wishlist tracker for online product pages. Single user, runs on my own machine, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20 with TypeScript
- Fastify for the HTTP server
- SQLite via better-sqlite3
- Server-rendered HTML with a small amount of vanilla JS, no React, no build step beyond tsc
- node-cron for scheduling checks
- Playwright (chromium) for fetching product pages, since plain fetch gets blocked

What it does:
1. A form where I paste a product URL, an optional nickname, and a target price.
2. On save, fetch the page once with Playwright, extract title, current price, currency and image using a per-domain extractor module with a generic fallback that looks at JSON-LD Product schema and og: meta tags.
3. Store a price_checks row every time a check runs, keyed to the item. Never overwrite history.
4. A cron job every 6 hours rechecks every active item, with a randomized delay of 5 to 40 seconds between items and a configurable user agent.
5. Dashboard lists items sorted by biggest drop from their own median price, showing current price, target, all-time low, and a small inline SVG sparkline drawn from price_checks.
6. Flag an item as 'hit' when current price is at or below target. Show hits in a pinned section at the top.
7. Optional notification via a NOTIFY_WEBHOOK env var: POST a JSON payload when an item first hits its target. Do not spam, only fire on transition into hit state.
8. CSV export of all items and price history at /export.

Explicitly out of scope: buying anything, cart, checkout, login to any retailer, affiliate links, multi-user support, mobile app.

Secrets and config in .env: PORT, NOTIFY_WEBHOOK, CHECK_CRON, USER_AGENT. Ship a .env.example.

Be honest in the README: scraping is fragile, per-domain extractors will break when sites change markup, and the generic JSON-LD fallback is the only thing that degrades gracefully. Include a single seeded example item so the dashboard is not empty on first run, and one vitest test for the JSON-LD extractor against a saved HTML fixture.
